newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Ireland asks EU to give impetus to treaty talks.
newsitem.headline: Ireland asks EU to give impetus to treaty talks.

text.p: Irish Prime Minister John Bruton told his European Union colleagues on Wednesday that they must use a special summit in Dublin at the weekend to give a push to the EU's preparations for the 21st century.
He also said the leaders must make sure that negotiations on a new EU treaty stay on track to finish in mid-June next year and no later.

In a letter inviting leaders from the 15 EU countries to the summit on Saturday, Bruton said the Union had to face up to massive global challenges that include population, food, health and environmental pressures and a communications revolution.

"As the Union embarks on its own ambitious tasks...it must satisfy itself that its political institutions are developed to retain the engagement, the respect and the active support of Union citizens," he wrote.
Tasks facing the Union included the introduction of a single currency and enlargement into eastern Europe and the Mediterranean, he said.

The summit is being held to meet the concerns of some in the EU -- notably French President Jacques Chirac -- that the inter-governmental conference (IGC), a treaty review preparing the bloc for enlargement, has become bogged down.
Bruton said, however, that he believed the talks were "reasonably well on track" to provide a draft treaty for leaders at the European Council in Dublin in December.
But he said that Saturday's meeting should give "political guidance and impetus" to the IGC and make sure that it stuck to a timetable for finishing in June next year.
Bruton said the meeting would begin with an informal lunch during which all concerned could express their opinions on the progress of the IGC.

It would be followed by a longer afternoon session during which Irish Foreign Minister Dick Spring, responsible for the IGC under the Irish EU presidency, would brief the leaders on where things stood.
The leaders would discuss a number of external matters over dinner, including the United States, Japan and Russia, Bruton said.
